analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans to cover second opinions for serious medical conditions at normal cost sharing.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to three House committees on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the laws governing employer health plans and health insurance to require coverage of a second medical opinion when a patient questions a diagnosis or treatment for a condition that threatens life, limb, bodily or cognitive function, or quality of life. Coverage would include at least three appointments with a qualified second-opinion physician plus related diagnostic tests, at the same cost sharing as an initial opinion. The bill would limit insurers' ability to restrict second opinions to in-network doctors (unless a qualified in-network doctor is available within 50 miles within 30 days), bar pre-approval requirements when delay could harm the patient, and require quick written notice, appeal rights, and public timelines for handling second-opinion claims.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients in employer plans or individual insurance who face a serious, uncertain, or non-improving diagnosis and want another doctor's view before committing to surgery or a treatment plan. They would get at least three covered appointments plus related tests, at ordinary co-pay levels, with protections against network restrictions and long approval delays. Physicians (including nurse practitioners) acting for patients could also request the second opinion with the patient's consent.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients facing serious or uncertain diagnoses

how_it_helps.text: Plans and insurers must cover a second opinion when a patient or their practitioner questions a diagnosis, treatment plan, surgery, or therapy for a condition threatening loss of life, limb, bodily or cognitive function, or quality of life, and in other listed situations such as conflicting test results or a treatment plan that is not working.
Coverage includes at least three appointments with a qualified second-opinion physician plus ancillary diagnostic tests, with patient cost sharing equal to a comparable initial in-network visit.

Plans may restrict second opinions to in-network physicians only if a qualified in-network physician is within 50 miles with an initial appointment within 30 days; pre-approval is barred when an imminent threat to health makes delay detrimental, and in those cases the plan must reimburse a patient who paid out of pocket.

Denials must be explained in writing within 3 business days, plans must establish an appeal process, and plans must file publicly available timelines for reimbursing second-opinion claims and responding to pre-approval requests.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employers and plan sponsors who fund group plans would bear the cost of additional covered visits and tests, plus new administrative duties (appeal processes, quick denial notices, and public timelines). Those costs would partly flow into premiums.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and employer plan sponsors

drawbacks.text: The bill adds a new mandatory benefit to group and individual plans, and the added claims would be paid by insurers and plan sponsors and would partly surface as higher premiums for everyone enrolled.

The triggers are broad: any condition that 'threatens loss of life, quality of life' or substantially impairs mind or body, including serious chronic conditions, could qualify, which leaves room for wide interpretation and increased use.

The bill layers additional administrative requirements (10-business-day pre-approval notice, 3-business-day denial notice, appeal processes, public timelines) onto plans already subject to ERISA, PHS Act, and Internal Revenue Code rules overseen by three separate departments, adding compliance burden even with a coordination provision.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and targeted: a patient about to undergo surgery or start a serious treatment gets a covered, reasonably timed second opinion instead of having to pay out of pocket or fight the insurer. The costs are genuine but modest — more covered visits and tests spread across all enrollees, plus compliance paperwork. The bill offsets costs by allowing in-network-only second opinions (when a qualified doctor is available promptly), pre-approval in non-urgent cases, and consultation-report requirements. On balance it is a narrow consumer protection, not a sweeping mandate.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees the day it was introduced and then to two subcommittees, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Susan Davis introduced the bill on May 18, 2009, joined by four original cosponsors, two Democrats and two Republicans.

The bill was referred the same day to the House Energy and Commerce, Education and Labor, and Ways and Means Committees, and in the following months to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health and the Education and Labor Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action was taken — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and the employers who sponsor group plans were better off because the bill never advanced: they avoided a new mandatory benefit and its associated administrative requirements. Patients with serious or uncertain diagnoses gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's small support base was evenly split: its sponsor was a Democrat, and its four cosponsors were two Democrats and two Republicans; no chamber-level vote ever split along party lines because none occurred.

industries.note: The bill would require insurers to pay for second-opinion visits and tests they can currently limit or deny, and to meet quick pre-approval, denial-notice, and appeal deadlines. An insurer's savings from discouraging second opinions is precisely the cost the bill would shift back onto coverage, so the industry's interest runs against the patient's.

industries.industry: Employers and plan sponsors funding group health plans
industries.note: ERISA group plans are typically funded by employers, who would absorb a new mandatory benefit and compliance duties, partly passed on as higher premium contributions.

Second-opinion physicians would receive reimbursed consultations (at least three appointments plus related tests), and treating practitioners could formally request a second opinion with the patient's consent, giving both sides a financially supported pathway.
